posts.title: Grateful on Thanksgiving
posts.description: Vintage ad 1942 I am filled with gratitude for the support and heart of this extraordinary community of readers, every single day, including today and I wish you all a wonderful Thanksgiving. I know for many of us today may be a difficult day, and feelings of loss can be felt so deeply. I send extra love to you. I give thanks for each and every one of you.

posts.title: What the Nevada Nuclear Tests Should Have Taught Us About Iowa.
posts.description: In the early 1950’s the Atomic Energy Commission decided that parts of Utah and Nevada would be the site of a continental proving ground for nuclear weapons. It became the first American Ground Zero. “Accidents Will Happen- By The Bombs Early Light.”Collage of appropriated images by Sally Edelstein As Iowa and the Midwest brace for the US Army to detonate ten tons of degraded lead azide, potentially releasing toxic lead particles into the atmosphere, one question eats at me. Has the government not learned anything from our nuclear tests and the Downwinders in the 1950s? Ask the folks in Utah; they know a little something about the consequences of our federal government putting dangerous substances into the atmosphere. The nuclear tests took place in Nevada, but radioactive fallout traveled throughout Utah and as far north as Idaho. Generations of families have suffered the consequences. posts.title: After 52 Years, My Voice Was Heard in Syracuse
posts.description: It took 52 years, but my voice was finally heard in Syracuse. A few weeks ago, Dave Bullard interviewed me for WRVO, an NPR station that serves Syracuse. We talked about the essay I wrote for HuffPost about being gang-raped at a fraternity house when I was an 18-year-old freshman at Syracuse University in 1974. I had almost forgotten about the interview until I woke up to an email message from a professor at the University of Arizona. She had just listened to it and wanted to thank me for sharing my story. Other public radio stations in New York had picked up the interview, and somehow my voice had made its way to a woman in Arizona. But knowing my story had been heard in Syracuse got to me. I kept thinking about the radios I listened to as a freshman, the ones that played “Bad Bad Leroy Brown” and Elton John’s “Bennie and the Jets.” I can still hear those songs.
